newsitem.title: UK: UK directors urge shareholder involvement -survey.
newsitem.headline: UK directors urge shareholder involvement -survey.

text.p: A survey of directors, chief executives and chairmen from Britain's top 250 companies shows they believe institutional shareholders should have greater influence in running the firms, executive recruitment firm Russell Reynolds Associates said on Thursday.

The group said half the directors interviewed in its MORI poll said institutional shareholders were not effective in terms of the impact they have on business practice and believe they should vote at company meetings and disclose their decisions.
The view was supported by 71 percent of the chairmen and CEOs interviewed for the survey. The report canvassed the views of 100 executive and non-executive directors.

"This research has exposed gaps in existing corporate governance guidelines and identified areas that should be subject to directives in the future," David Shellard, managing director of the group said in a statement.

Shellard said a momentum had developed "which reflects a wider mood for change". "Many of the views expressed...show strong support for companies to adopt greater disclosure and transparency," he added in a summary of the survey.

The survey found that long-term performance bonuses were the most favoured remuneration method for executive directors, supported by 98 percent of executive directors and 84 percent percent non-executives.
But 74 percent of executive directors and 94 percent of non-executive directors opposed long-term performance bonuses for non-executive directors, the survey found.

It said 88 percent of directors believed the Cadbury Report on corporate governance "has had a significant influence on how British companies run their affairs". But only 64 percent said the Greenbury report on executive pay had been influential.
The survey said 32 percent of executives and 22 percent of non-executives claim that the supervisory role of non-executives is not effective.
And more than a third of all directors surveyed would like to see the establishment of consistent performance criteria.
The report also said that 70 percent of directors "would like to see directors of major companies".
